subsystems.name: Lift envelope
subsystems.role: a huge gas-tight hull that floats because its contents are lighter than Venus's dense carbon dioxide.

subsystems.name: Habitat deck
subsystems.role: pressurised, shirt-sleeve living and working space for the crew.

subsystems.name: Power system
subsystems.role: collects near-continuous sunlight above the haze and stores it for the dark side of the circuit.

subsystems.name: Altitude and attitude control
subsystems.role: keeps the craft in the narrow temperate layer and holds it steady for docking.

subsystems.name: Shuttles and ascent vehicle
subsystems.role: smaller airships and a rocket that carries people and cargo between the habitat, the deep atmosphere and orbit.

subsystems.name: Communications and navigation
subsystems.role: links the drifting city to orbit, Earth and any surface assets.

buildSteps.title: Test the envelope material
buildSteps.detail: Candidate fabrics would be soaked in sulfuric acid aerosol under ultraviolet light for months to prove they survive the cloud deck.

buildSteps.title: Fly robotic precursors
buildSteps.detail: Small aerostats would drift in the clouds for weeks or longer, measuring winds, chemistry and structural loads that no mission has recorded for more than a couple of days.

buildSteps.title: Size the hull around the crew's own air
buildSteps.detail: Because a nitrogen–oxygen mix is buoyant in carbon dioxide, the habitat atmosphere itself can supply lift; the hull volume is set by the mass it must carry, with generous margin.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate and pack the envelope
buildSteps.detail: The hull is built in sections, seam-sealed and folded into an aeroshell small enough for launch.

buildSteps.title: Pre-position cargo
buildSteps.detail: Robotic flights deliver supplies, spares and the ascent rocket ahead of the crew, so nothing essential arrives on the same vehicle as the people.

buildSteps.title: Enter and inflate
buildSteps.detail: An aeroshell brakes in the upper atmosphere; after parachute descent the envelope is deployed and filled at the target altitude, then the craft begins drifting with the winds.

buildSteps.title: Bring the crew down
buildSteps.detail: A capsule descends from orbit and docks with the drifting habitat, where the envelope and life-support systems are already running.

buildSteps.title: Operate and rotate crews
buildSteps.detail: The city circles the planet every few Earth days, staying near constant sunlight; crews rotate using a rocket launched from beneath the hull, which needs far less energy than launching from the surface.

prerequisites.tech: Buoyant aerostats in the Venus clouds
prerequisites.why: two balloons floated in the Venus atmosphere for roughly two days in 1985; nothing has flown there since, so long-duration behaviour is unproven.
the clouds are sulfuric acid droplets, and no material has been qualified to hold a pressurised envelope there for years.
orbital stations recycle water and some air, but a remote settlement would need far higher closure with no resupply for months.

prerequisites.tech: Ascent from the cloud deck to orbit
prerequisites.why: no vehicle has ever climbed from Venus's atmosphere to orbit; the habitat's drifting platform would be the launch pad.
probes and orbiters have worked there, but precision delivery to a specific altitude and continuous relay coverage are harder.
solar arrays work in space and Venus receives more sunlight than Earth, but they must be built light enough to fly on an airship.

pathway.milestone: orbiter and atmospheric-probe missions in development to re-measure the clouds and surface
pathway.unlocks: modern data on winds, chemistry and materials exposure after decades without it.

pathway.milestone: a long-lived robotic airship that survives months in the cloud layer
pathway.unlocks: proven envelope materials, lift-gas handling and autonomous flight.

pathway.milestone: a crewed expedition of weeks to months in a floating habitat
pathway.unlocks: human factors, radiation exposure and resupply experience.
a second habitable world, if acid-resistant materials and closed-loop life support can be made to last.
